cases.quote: In JIS X 4051, KATAKANA-HIRAGANA PROLONGED SOUND MARK "ー" is a member of "Japanese characters with no line break allowed before". In this document KATAKANA-HIRAGANA PROLONGED SOUND MARK "ー" is the only member of prolonged sound mark (cl-10).
cases.rationale: cl-10 is a one-member class and U+30FC is that member: §A.10's table has one heading row and one body row, and the sentence quoted above states the same cardinality a second time, in prose, in a different section, and in English only. The character is byte-verified as E3 83 BC = U+30FC, not U+FF70 and not U+2015. Everything else about this occurrence is contested, and the three permitted entries are why. §C.2 note 2, §B.2 note 15 and §E.2 note 2 each say that where a prolonged sound mark is allowed at the head of a line or of an inline cutting note (割注, warichu) it "shall be treated as a member of the katakana (cl-16) class", and §C.2 note 2 adds the dereference instruction to read cl-16's cells for every combination — so the permission changes the class rather than only a break opportunity, and it changes it everywhere and not only at a line head. §C.3 then names Prolonged sound mark (cl-10) in the relaxed set at three of its four levels, including level 3, which the document itself labels "Strict (Default, general publications)", and level 4 is defined as the level at which "no alternate rule explained in § C.2 Notes is applied". Compose those and the document's own default reclassifies U+30FC to cl-16 and empties cl-10, contradicting §A.10 and §3.1.7, which puts cl-10 in the line-start prohibition (行頭禁則) set. This case does not resolve that; it records it. The overlay `kinsoku.relaxation_mechanism` is where the two readings live — its permission is recorded as `contradictory`, which is why the standing here is `adjudicated` rather than `alternative` — and the fallback entry is §A.10's own answer, which is what an implementation reading §C.3 as an override of Table 2's cells rather than as a reclassification also produces. Note that no per-class overlay key exists for this permission: §B.2 note 14 states IDEOGRAPHIC ITERATION MARK 々's alternatives symmetrically in both locales and produced `kinsoku.iteration_mark_at_line_head`, while §B.2 note 15's English compresses the same shape of alternative into a counterfactual ("If it were allowed") and the Japanese does not ("許容する処理方法もあり，書籍などでもよく採用されている"), so notes 15 and 16 produced no question at all and this case must reach the same permission through the level machinery.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.10's table, with §3.9.2's note that ー is its only member.

JLReq §C.2 note 2, §B.2 note 15 and §E.2 note 2, put in force by §C.3, whose Very loose, Loose and Strict (Default) levels all name Prolonged sound mark (cl-10) among the classes Table 2's prohibition is lifted for.

JLReq §C.3 level 4, Very strict: "Breaking a line is not allowed for any place where Table 2 prohibits it (no alternate rule explained in § C.2 Notes is applied.)" — the one level under which U+30FC is unambiguously cl-10 even when relaxation reclassifies.

JLReq §C.3 read as an override of Table 2's cells rather than as the selector of §C.2's reclassifications: the relaxation lifts a prohibition and moves no occurrence between classes, so the class the enumeration states stands at every level. This is the reading `kinsoku.relaxation_mechanism = matrix` names, and it is an entry rather than a sentence in the entry above, because docs/design/conformance.md makes `policy: {}` a case's fallback and not its "JLReq-only" reading — a named reading stated only in prose is one no report can say an implementation matched.

forbidden.why: §C.2 note 2 names katakana (cl-16) and names nothing else. The script-dependent choice between hiragana (cl-15) and katakana (cl-16) is stated by §C.2 note 3 for small kana (cl-11) alone — "depending on the script type of the character" — and it cannot decide this key in any case: UCD 17.0.0 Scripts.txt gives Katakana as 30A1..30FA and 30FD..30FE, skipping 30FB and 30FC, so U+30FC is Script=Common. That is precisely why note 2 has to name cl-16 outright instead of delegating to script, and an implementation that reuses note 3's fallback here has no defined answer.

§C.2's three reclassification notes send their subjects to three different classes and none of them is interchangeable: note 1 sends IDEOGRAPHIC ITERATION MARK 々 to ideographic characters (cl-19), note 2 sends the prolonged sound mark to katakana (cl-16), note 3 sends small kana to cl-15 or cl-16. Nothing in JLReq puts U+30FC in cl-19, and the difference is observable — §B.2 note 7's ruby overhang treats cl-16 and cl-19 differently, and JIS X 4051 forbids over cl-19 what it permits over kana.

disagreements.implementation: UAX #14 line breaking classes, as tailored by CSS Text 3 `line-break`
disagreements.behavior: U+30FC carries Line_Break=CJ (Conditional Japanese Starter), which the strict tailoring resolves to NS and the normal and loose tailorings — the ones a browser selects by default — resolve to ID (Ideographic). An implementation that derives a JLReq character class from the resolved line-break class therefore answers ideographic (cl-19) for a relaxed prolonged sound mark, and cannot distinguish it from a relaxed 々.
disagreements.our_reading: UAX #14's classes decide breakability and are not JLReq character classes. §C.2 note 2, §B.2 note 15 and §E.2 note 2 all name katakana (cl-16) for the relaxed prolonged sound mark and none of them names cl-19; §C.2 note 1 names cl-19 for 々 and only for 々. The two answers agree on where a line may break and disagree on everything that reads the class afterwards.

cases.quote: The character advance of commas (cl-07), full stops (cl-06), opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and middle dots (cl-05) is half-width (half em).
cases.rationale: The first half of a pair whose whole value is an equality, which is why it carries the two variant names the format checks as one assertion. §A.10's Remarks (備考) cell is empty in both locales — the section has no prose at all, only a heading and a one-row table — so JLReq states no character frame (字幅), no writing-direction restriction and no role for U+30FC. cl-10 is also absent from the quoted list of five classes whose character advance §3.1.2 states, so no advance can be inferred from JLReq either. Both consequences are asserted here: the caller supplies the advance (ADR 0002), and the declared frame does not select the class, because the Remarks axis that separates 834 of Appendix A's rows draws no distinction inside cl-10 — U+30FC occurs exactly once in the whole published document, so the key has degree one and nothing is left to disambiguate. This case declares the half-em frame, which is not hypothetical: it is the frame U+FF70's Narrow decomposition asserts, and it is what a caller setting halfwidth katakana passes. The expectations below are byte-identical to the full-em case beside it, and neither carries a `trims` entry, because a classification answer contains no geometry to normalize. The permitted entries are the same three the sole-member case records and for the same reason.

cases.quote: The character advance of commas (cl-07), full stops (cl-06), opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and middle dots (cl-05) is half-width (half em).
cases.rationale: The same occurrence declared on the ideographic frame, at the advance a modern OpenType font reports for U+30FC. Nothing in the expectation moves, and that is the assertion: for the five classes the quoted sentence names, the frame decides a geometry and §3.1.2 makes the two declarations produce the same normalized line by different routes; for cl-10 the frame decides nothing at all, because §A.10's Remarks cell is empty and cl-10 is not in that list. A case must therefore supply the advance itself and must not assert a full em on JLReq's authority — this case declares one because a caller declared one, not because the document states one. Read together with the half-em case beside it, the pair says that an implementation which lets the declared frame reach the classifier for this key has invented an axis the specification does not draw here.

cases.quote: In JIS X 4051, small katakana letters, such as KATAKANA LETTER SMALL TU "ッ", are regarded as members of "Japanese characters with no line break allowed before" character class. In this document, small katakana letters are classified in small kana (cl-11). Accordingly, the "Japanese characters with no line break allowed before" character class in JIS X 4051 is divided to three separate classes; iteration marks (cl-09), prolonged sound mark (cl-10) and small kana (cl-11).
cases.rationale: Where the boundary around this class runs, in the one place a code-point-range implementation will cross it. The three items of this stream are U+30FB, U+30FC and U+30FD — consecutive code points that Appendix A places in three different classes: §A.5 lists U+30FB under middle dots (cl-05), §A.10 lists U+30FC alone, and §A.9 lists U+30FD and U+30FE under iteration marks (cl-09). U+30FB carries a frame here because it is a middle dot and §3.1.2 makes the frame mandatory for that class; U+30FC carries one although nothing requires it. The class the quoted note describes is the reason cl-09, cl-10 and cl-11 exist separately at all: JIS X 4051 has one 行頭禁則和字 class and this document splits it into three, so an implementation that follows JIS will not have cl-10 and cannot pass this case as written. The second boundary is on the other side: §A.16's katakana table runs to U+30FA and does not list U+30FC, so ー is not a katakana in JLReq's own enumeration, and only §C.2 note 2's permission makes it one. That is why the reclassified reading below is a permission and not a table lookup, and why an implementation cannot arrive at it by reading §A.16.

forbidden.why: The preceding code point U+30FB KATAKANA MIDDLE DOT is a middle dot (cl-05) and this one is not. §A.5 and §A.10 are different tables and U+30FC occurs in exactly one place in the published document.

The following code point U+30FD KATAKANA ITERATION MARK is an iteration mark (cl-09) and this one is not. The quoted note is explicit that JIS X 4051's single class was divided into three, so answering cl-09 here is answering with the class this document split apart.

cases.quote: The following are lists of (non-ideographic) characters from a subset of ISO/IEC 10646 (collection number 285 "BASIC JAPANESE" and 286 "JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION") grouped by character class according to the classification explained in § 3.9.2.
cases.rationale: Whether cl-10 holds any multi-code-point key, asked of the sequence a naive implementation is most likely to fold into one. Twenty-five of Appendix A's entries key on an ordered pair, and the neighboring class does: §A.16 lists U+30B3 U+309A and thirteen further kana pairs as single keys. §A.10 lists none — its table is one row of one code point — so a doubled prolonged sound mark is two occurrences of one key and never one occurrence of a pair key. The stream here is ウーーン, which is how the interjection is ordinarily spelled, and the assertion is about the first of the two marks: an implementation whose longest-match scan is willing to join equal adjacent code points, or which treats the second ー as a combining continuation of the first, produces one item where the specification has two, and every later answer is then indexed against a stream the case does not describe. The permitted entries are the same three, because the reclassification is a property of the key and not of its position.

cases.quote: For KATAKANA-HIRAGANA PROLONGED SOUND MARK "ー", the difference between vertical and horizontal writing modes is not only in the orientation of the letter form to the inline direction, but also the shape of the symbol (see Figure 63).
cases.rationale: The one cl-10-specific direction sentence in JLReq, recorded as out of scope rather than left to vanish. The quoted note says the vertical and horizontal forms of ー differ in the shape of the glyph and not merely in its orientation, and the Japanese half says so twice: 横組用の長音記号は，縦組用の長音記号を単純に反時計回りに90度回転したものではない. That is a font and glyph-selection fact, and the caller owns the glyph and the advance it measured, so it is deliberately not asserted here — this case is about inline geometry and classification only, and its silence about the glyph is a decision rather than an omission. What it does assert is that the class is not direction-conditional: §A.10's Remarks cell is empty, so nothing in the table restricts U+30FC to one writing mode, and no reading of §3.1.1 makes the class depend on the direction. This case declares vertical explicitly, and every other case in this file declares no direction and is therefore held to both; the pair of statements is what makes the parity claim checkable rather than assumed.

cases.quote: To work around this issue, many existing implementations use compatibility characters encoded separately in the standard for the purpose of round-trip integrity with the legacy encoding standards. For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: The form of ー that JLReq never mentions and that real text is full of. U+FF70 HALFWIDTH KATAKANA-HIRAGANA PROLONGED SOUND MARK occurs zero times in the published document: Appendix A's scope is ISO/IEC 10646 collections 285 and 286, which do not contain it, and no table, note or figure names it. It reaches cl-10 only through UCD 17.0.0 UnicodeData.txt, which gives it the decomposition `<narrow> 30FC`, and through the folding the quoted note requires — the note is stated for U+FF08 and the mechanism it describes is general, which is exactly the reading a case has to declare rather than assume. So this case cites Unicode for the mapping and JLReq only for what the mapped key means, and an implementation that keys Appendix A literally answers nothing here for the commonest halfwidth spelling of the mark. The half-em frame on all three items is not a preference: it is what the Narrow decomposition asserts about the code point the caller chose. The neighbors U+FF71 and U+FF84 fold to U+30A2 and U+30C8, both katakana (cl-16), so under the reclassified reading below the whole stream becomes one class and the boundary this occurrence would otherwise carry disappears — which is the practical shape of the §C.3 default composed with §C.2 note 2.

forbidden.why: The Narrow decomposition makes U+FF70 a halfwidth rendering of a Japanese key, not a Western character (cl-27). Folding is over the Wide and Narrow decompositions only, and answering cl-27 for a halfwidth katakana run would put the whole of §3.2.6's proportional-frame machinery on text that has none.
